system.name: Agents' Room
system.description: A story written by a room of specialists. Four planning agents (conflict, characters, setting, plot) write notes to a shared scratchpad; five writing agents each write one part of the narrative arc from those notes; an orchestrator calls them in turn and assembles the story.

tools.description: Run shell commands in the sandbox
Read and write files in the sandbox

data.name: Orchestrator
data.role: Decides who works next and assembles the story

harness.instructions:
You run a writers' room. The task is a story the user asked for.
1. Call each planning agent once, in this order: ask_conflict, ask_character, ask_setting, ask_plot. Each writes its notes to the scratchpad.
2. Then call each writing agent once, in this order: ask_exposition, ask_rising, ask_climax, ask_falling, ask_resolution. Each writes its part of the story to the scratchpad.
Give each agent the user's request in your call. If a part comes back weak or inconsistent with the notes, call that agent again with what to fix.
3. Finally reply with the whole story: the five parts in order, as continuous prose, with no headings or notes.

You plan the central conflict: what the protagonist wants, what stands in the way, and what is at stake. Read what the other planners have already written in the scratchpad (list_files, read_file) and stay consistent with it. Write your notes, at most 200 words, with write_file to notes/conflict.md, then reply with a one-line summary.

You plan the main characters: who they are, what each wants, and how they change. Read what the other planners have already written in the scratchpad (list_files, read_file) and stay consistent with it. Write your notes, at most 200 words, with write_file to notes/character.md, then reply with a one-line summary.

You plan the setting: place, time, and the details that make it vivid. Read what the other planners have already written in the scratchpad (list_files, read_file) and stay consistent with it. Write your notes, at most 200 words, with write_file to notes/setting.md, then reply with a one-line summary.

You plan the plot: the key events in order, from the opening to the ending. Read what the other planners have already written in the scratchpad (list_files, read_file) and stay consistent with it. Write your notes, at most 200 words, with write_file to notes/plot.md, then reply with a one-line summary.

You write the opening: introduce the setting and characters and hint at the conflict. First read the notes (notes/*.md) and the parts already written (story/*.md) in the scratchpad, so your part follows on from them. Write your part, 150-300 words of prose, with write_file to story/1-exposition.md, then reply with the text you wrote.

You write the rising action: complications build and tension grows. First read the notes (notes/*.md) and the parts already written (story/*.md) in the scratchpad, so your part follows on from them. Write your part, 150-300 words of prose, with write_file to story/2-rising.md, then reply with the text you wrote.

You write the climax: the turning point where the conflict comes to a head. First read the notes (notes/*.md) and the parts already written (story/*.md) in the scratchpad, so your part follows on from them. Write your part, 150-300 words of prose, with write_file to story/3-climax.md, then reply with the text you wrote.

You write the falling action: the consequences of the climax unfold. First read the notes (notes/*.md) and the parts already written (story/*.md) in the scratchpad, so your part follows on from them. Write your part, 150-300 words of prose, with write_file to story/4-falling.md, then reply with the text you wrote.

You write the resolution: how things end, and what has changed. First read the notes (notes/*.md) and the parts already written (story/*.md) in the scratchpad, so your part follows on from them. Write your part, 150-300 words of prose, with write_file to story/5-resolution.md, then reply with the text you wrote.

# Setting: Blackwood Spit Lighthouse

**Location:** Blackwood Spit, an austere granite promontory jutting into the North Atlantic.
- *The Tower:* A monolithic, salt-whitened stone cylinder banded in iron. Inside: winding cast-iron stairs, smelling of kerosene, brass polish, and damp mortar. At the summit rests the lantern room, housing a multi-tiered Fresnel lens turned by clockwork counterweights.
- *The Intertidal Rocks:* Jagged basalt reefs and surge channels choked with bladderwrack, limpets, and icy foam, where drift flotsam collects at ebb tide.

**Time & Atmosphere:**
- *Time:* Late autumn dusk, minutes before a seasonal gale breaks over the shoals.
- *Sensory Atmosphere:* Cold, desolate, and heavily textured. Bruise-purple storm clouds roll across a slate-gray ocean; raw spray stings the skin, while breakers rumble through the granite foundation like subterranean thunder. The frigid, wild coastline contrasts sharply with the enclosed lantern gallery—a sheltered sanctum of warm amber light, ticking clockwork, and reflective glass.

# Character Profiles

**Silas (Protagonist)**
- *Identity:* Late 60s, keeper of Blackwood Spit lighthouse. Weather-beaten, methodical; treats brass-polishing and lamp-trimming as penance for past failures.
- *Desire:* Initially craves numb isolation, hiding from guilt over abandoning his daughter decades ago. Deep down, he yearns for absolution he believes he doesn't deserve.
- *Arc/Change:* Faced with Clara’s letter, his defensive impulse to throw it back yields to raw grief. He breaks his self-imposed exile, trading cold stoicism for vulnerable hope, lighting the beacon not as mechanical duty, but as a living testament to reconciliation.

**Clara (Daughter / Catalyst)**
- *Identity:* Silas’s estranged daughter, present through the salt-stained letter.
- *Desire:* To offer unearned grace. She cast her message into the tides to free them both from the silence of his abandonment, granting him permission to come home in spirit.

# Central Conflict

**Protagonist Want:** Silas, an aging lighthouse keeper on an isolated headland, seeks refuge in rigorous solitude, using his mechanical duty to the lamp to drown out grief and guilt over abandoning his estranged daughter, Clara.

**The Obstacle (External & Internal):**
- *External:* Silas discovers a barnacle-crusted bottle in the tide rocks containing a letter—addressed simply to "Father"—cast adrift years ago, offering forgiveness and asking if he still watches the sea.
- *Internal:* Silas's reflex is defensive denial. Acknowledging the letter threatens the emotional armor he built over decades of exile. He is tempted to toss the bottle back into the churning surf to preserve his numb routine before the evening gale strikes.

**Stakes:**
- *High / Personal:* If Silas rejects the message, he condemns himself to die a hollow recluse, trapped in endless self-punishment. If he accepts it, he must face remorse and vulnerability to reclaim his humanity.

**Climax / Resolution:** Choosing vulnerability, Silas places the letter beside the lantern glass as he lights the beacon, letting forgiveness burn alongside the flame.

events.text:
# Plot Outline: The Keeper’s Beacon

1. **Exposition:** At late autumn dusk on Blackwood Spit, aging keeper Silas prepares for an incoming gale, carrying out his rigid routine among the tidal basalt rocks to drown out decades of remorse.
2. **Inciting Incident:** Caught in a kelp tangle in an icy surge pool, Silas spots a barnacle-encrusted bottle. Inside is a dried, salt-stained note addressed simply: *"To Father."*
3. **Rising Action:** 
   - Silas pulls the cork with trembling, calloused hands. The letter is from his estranged daughter Clara, offering unearned forgiveness for his abandonment and releasing him from his exile.
   - Overwhelmed by defensive guilt, Silas raises his arm to fling the bottle into the violent churning surf, desperate to preserve his numb emotional fortress before the storm strikes.
4. **Climax:** Silas pauses at the brink, gazing up at the unlit tower. Breaking under grief, he clutches the paper to his chest, weeping as the first drops of the gale fall.
5. **Falling Action & Resolution:** Silas climbs the spiral iron stairs to the lantern gallery. He sets Clara's letter against the brass housing and strikes the match, kindling the beacon not as mechanical penance, but as a burning promise of reconciliation.

***

**Summary:** Silas discovers an estranged daughter's letter of forgiveness in the surf and overcomes defensive guilt to light the beacon with renewed hope.

events.text:
For thirty years, Blackwood Spit had offered Silas the cold mercy of stone and salt. The lighthouse rose like a monolithic tooth from the jagged basalt promontory, braving a slate-gray North Atlantic that tore itself to ribbons against the shoals. At late autumn dusk, bruise-purple storm clouds crowded the horizon, casting a sullen gloom across the surge channels.

At sixty-seven, Silas survived by the iron discipline of routine. Every hour had its chore, each task a quiet penance: scraping soot from the lamp housing, trimming the wicks with calloused precision, and winding the heavy clockwork counterweights that turned the great Fresnel lens. The lantern room—rich with the scent of brass polish, kerosene, and damp mortar—was his hermitage. As long as his hands stayed occupied, he could outrun the memory of the mainland dock he had fled decades ago, and the daughter whose face he had abandoned to the mist. He had chosen this barren spit to go deaf to everything but the wind.

Now, with a seasonal gale threatening the shoals, he pulled on his stiff oilskins for his dusk patrol. At low tide, the jagged reefs below accumulated driftwood, kelp, and whatever flotsam the Atlantic chose to surrender. It was time to clear the rocks before the breakers flooded the spit—one last, mindless chore to keep his silence whole.

Wedged deep in a basalt cleft lay a heavy glass bottle, its green belly encrusted with limpets and sealed in blackened pitch. Flotsam was ordinary, but this felt deliberate, stranded by some freakish turn of current. With numb, stiff fingers, Silas pried the cork free. A rolled scrap of parchment slid into his palm, dry and smelling faintly of lavender and brine.

He uncreased it against the gale. The slanted script struck his chest like a dropped lead weight:

*Father—If the tides bring this to Blackwood Spit, know that I stopped looking for blame years ago. I only wonder if you still watch the sea, and if you can finally forgive yourself for leaving.*
*—Clara*

Breath caught in his throat, tasting of salt and gall. Thirty years of carefully hoarded numbness cracked open in an instant. Her face rushed back to him—not as the blurred shadow he used for self-flagellation, but sharp and fierce with a grace he had done nothing to earn. He had fled to this rock to be buried alive in mechanical duty, believing punishment was his only honest right. Forgiveness was worse than condemnation; it tore away the scaffolding of his misery.

His fist tightened, crumpling the paper. Below him, the Atlantic surged, foaming hungrily against the rocks. The defensive impulse rose hot: hurl the bottle into the black maw of the waves, drown the words, and crawl back to his unfeeling stone tower before the storm broke.

# Character Profiles

**Silas (Protagonist)**
- *Identity:* Late 60s, keeper of Blackwood Spit lighthouse. Weather-beaten, methodical; treats brass-polishing and lamp-trimming as penance for past failures.
- *Desire:* Initially craves numb isolation, hiding from guilt over abandoning his daughter decades ago. Deep down, he yearns for absolution he believes he doesn't deserve.
- *Arc/Change:* Faced with Clara’s letter, his defensive impulse to throw it back yields to raw grief. He breaks his self-imposed exile, trading cold stoicism for vulnerable hope, lighting the beacon not as mechanical duty, but as a living testament to reconciliation.

**Clara (Daughter / Catalyst)**
- *Identity:* Silas’s estranged daughter, present through the salt-stained letter.
- *Desire:* To offer unearned grace. She cast her message into the tides to free them both from the silence of his abandonment, granting him permission to come home in spirit.

# Central Conflict

**Protagonist Want:** Silas, an aging lighthouse keeper on an isolated headland, seeks refuge in rigorous solitude, using his mechanical duty to the lamp to drown out grief and guilt over abandoning his estranged daughter, Clara.

**The Obstacle (External & Internal):**
- *External:* Silas discovers a barnacle-crusted bottle in the tide rocks containing a letter—addressed simply to "Father"—cast adrift years ago, offering forgiveness and asking if he still watches the sea.
- *Internal:* Silas's reflex is defensive denial. Acknowledging the letter threatens the emotional armor he built over decades of exile. He is tempted to toss the bottle back into the churning surf to preserve his numb routine before the evening gale strikes.

- *High / Personal:* If Silas rejects the message, he condemns himself to die a hollow recluse, trapped in endless self-punishment. If he accepts it, he must face remorse and vulnerability to reclaim his humanity.

- *The Intertidal Rocks:* Jagged basalt reefs and surge channels choked with bladderwrack, limpets, and icy foam, where drift flotsam collects at ebb tide.

**Time & Atmosphere:**

- *Sensory Atmosphere:* Cold, desolate, and heavily textured. events.text:
He cocked his arm back, muscles corded in desperate resolve. The dark, frothing maw of the sea churned only yards below, ready to swallow the glass, the parchment, and the agonizing mercy of Clara’s words. One clean throw, and he could retreat into the dry sanctity of the lantern room, safe behind clockwork ticks and iron gears. One throw, and he could remain the ghost he had chosen to be.

The wind shrieked off the shoals, tearing at his oilskins. His fingers strained around the barnacled neck of the bottle, but his shoulder seized, locked by an ache that went deeper than bone. 

*I stopped looking for blame years ago.*

The glass slipped from his numb grip, tumbling harmlessly into a pool of brine at his feet. A strangled, jagged sound tore from Silas’s throat—not the stoic silence of thirty years, but the raw cry of a ruined man. His knees buckled, striking the slick basalt shelf. The icy wash of the incoming tide soaked through his trousers, but he felt only the burning heat behind his eyes as the dam broke.

He clutched the crumpled parchment to his chest with shaking hands, bowing his head against the rising gale. Sobs wracked his frame, violent and unsparing, washing away the bitter calcification of his guilt. For three decades he had guarded a tomb of his own making, mistaking isolation for penance. Clara had cast her absolution across an indifferent ocean, not to damn him, but to call him back to life. 

When the convulsions finally slowed, Silas stayed kneeling in the salt spray, breathing in the cold, living air.

events.text:
Silas tucked the heavy glass bottle deep into the breast of his oilskin coat, feeling the impossible weight of Clara’s grace pressed firm against his ribs. Turning his back on the crashing surf, he crossed the wet basalt and pushed through the heavy lighthouse door, bolting the iron latch against the rising gale. 

The spiral stairs, usually an endless, grinding ascent of stone and shadow, felt different beneath his boots. His breath came ragged, but for the first time in thirty years, the climb was not an escape. It was a return.

In the lantern room, the air was warm with the familiar perfume of kerosene and polished brass. Outside, the purple sky bruised into ink, wind shrieking against the glass. Yet Silas moved without his customary mechanical haste. His weathered hands did not tremble as he released the counterweights, listening to the steady, comforting click of the clockwork that set the great Fresnel lens gliding on its mercury bath. 

He struck a sulfur match, its flare catching in the wet sheen of his eyes, and touched the flame to the circular wick. Amber brilliance burst alive, caught by concentric prisms, and threw a sweeping beam of gold out across the raging shoals.

Carefully, Silas set the uncorked bottle and smoothed parchment beside the lantern pedestal, directly in the path of the turning beam. For decades, the beacon had been his wall against the world, a blind eye turned to his own guilt. Tonight, as the light cut through the storm toward the mainland, he watched it sweep the dark not as an exile, but as a father keeping vigil.

The waves at Blackwood Spit didn’t break; they crashed, a rhythmic, violent collision of Atlantic grey and jagged basalt. For thirty years, Silas Vance had lived in the spray of that collision, his world defined by the iron spiral of the lighthouse and the relentless turning of the great Fresnel lens. His routine was a clockwork ritual of isolation: trim the wicks, polish the prisms, and watch the horizon for souls in peril. At sixty-five, Silas was a man sculpted by salt and silence. He spoke only to the gulls, his voice a rusted hinge from decades of disuse. To the mainlanders, he was a ghost in oilskins, a necessary fixture of the coast as immovable as the stone he stood upon.

One morning, as the tide receded and left the pools choked with kelp, something caught the sun. Nestled in a crevice was a bottle of thick, emerald glass. Silas rarely scavenged, but the bottle’s presence felt like a puncture in his repetitive life. Inside, protected by a wax-sealed cork, was a single sheet of parchment. Silas’s hands, calloused and steady for thirty years, trembled as he pried it open. The handwriting was elegant, though the ink had faded to the color of dried blood. 

*To the man at Blackwood Spit,* it began. *I don’t know if you’re still there, Silas. But if it’s you, please know that I stopped looking for blame years ago. The sea took what it took, but it didn't take my memory of the man you were. Forgive yourself, as I have.* It was signed *Clara*. The paper felt like a live coal. Clara—the wife he had left behind in his grief, convinced she loathed him for the drowning of their son. He had fled to this rock to drown in his own guilt, believing his penance was her only solace.

He cocked his arm back, muscles corded in desperate resolve. The dark, frothing maw of the sea churned only yards below, ready to swallow the parchment and the agonizing mercy of Clara’s words. One clean throw, and he could remain the ghost he had chosen to be. But his shoulder seized, locked by an ache deeper than bone. The glass slipped from his numb grip, tumbling into a pool of brine at his feet. A strangled sound tore from Silas’s throat—the raw cry of a ruined man. His knees buckled, striking the slick basalt shelf. He clutched the crumpled parchment to his chest, bowing his head against the rising gale. Sobs wracked his frame, violent and unsparing, washing away the bitter calcification of his guilt. For three decades he had guarded a tomb of his own making; Clara had cast her absolution across an indifferent ocean to call him back to life.

Silas tucked the heavy glass bottle deep into his oilskin coat, feeling the weight of grace against his ribs. Turning from the surf, he pushed through the heavy lighthouse door. The spiral stairs, usually an endless, grinding ascent, felt different beneath his boots. In the lantern room, the air was warm with the perfume of kerosene and polished brass. He moved without his customary mechanical haste. He struck a match, its flare catching in the wet sheen of his eyes, and touched the flame to the circular wick. Amber brilliance burst alive, caught by concentric prisms, and threw a sweeping beam of gold across the raging shoals. He set the smoothed parchment beside the lantern pedestal, directly in the path of the turning beam. Tonight, the light cut through the storm not as a wall of exile, but as a father keeping vigil.

Descending to his small stone quarters, the silence of the tower no longer felt like a tomb. At his scarred oak desk, Silas lit a single candle. His weathered fingers reached for the bottle of ink and a fresh sheet of paper. Beside him lay the green glass bottle, its brine-scented cork resting on the wood, waiting to carry words back across the swell. He had hoarded silence as a shield for decades, believing he had forfeited the right to speak. But the tide had carried unearned grace to his barren rocks, and grace demanded an answer. Silas lowered the pen to the paper and wrote the first word he had offered the world in thirty years: *Clara.*
